     6	# Report Generator
     7	
     8	Create professional, data-driven reports with charts, tables, and narrative text. Perfect for business reports, analytics dashboards, status updates, and automated reporting pipelines.
     9	
    10	## Quick Start
    11	
    12	```python
    13	from scripts.report_gen import ReportGenerator
    14	
    15	# Create a simple report
    16	report = ReportGenerator("Monthly Sales Report")
    17	report.add_text("This report summarizes sales performance for Q4 2024.")
    18	report.add_table(sales_data, title="Sales by Region")
    19	report.add_chart(sales_data, chart_type="bar", title="Revenue by Month")
    20	report.add_text("Key findings: Revenue increased 25% quarter-over-quarter.")
    21	report.generate().save("sales_report.pdf")
    22	
    23	# From template
    24	report = ReportGenerator.from_template("executive_summary")
    25	report.set_data(data_dict)
    26	report.generate().save("exec_summary.pdf")
    27	```
    28	
    29	## Features
    30	
    31	- **Multiple Output Formats**: PDF, HTML
    32	- **Rich Content**: Text, tables, charts, images, headers
    33	- **Chart Types**: Bar, line, pie, scatter, area, heatmap
    34	- **Table Formatting**: Auto-styling, conditional formatting
    35	- **Templates**: Pre-built report templates
    36	- **Branding**: Logo, colors, fonts, headers/footers
    37	- **Sections**: Table of contents, page numbers, appendices
    38	- **Data Integration**: CSV, DataFrame, dict inputs

     3	## About the Dataset
     4	
     5	This dataset, sourced from Kaggle (alitaqishah/global-cost-of-living-crisis-index-2026), provides a comprehensive snapshot of economic pressure and cost-of-living conditions across **80 major cities** worldwide. Each row represents a single city, with 22 columns capturing cost indices, income levels, rent burdens, inflation rates, and crisis classifications. All index values are benchmarked against New York, USA (index = 100).
     6	
     7	**Key facts:**
     8	- **Rows:** 80 (one per city)
     9	- **Columns:** 22
    10	- **Data year:** 2026
    11	- **Baseline reference:** New York, USA (index = 100)
    12	
    13	## Column Schema
    14	
    15	| Column Name | Type | Description |
    16	|---|---|---|
    17	| rank | Integer | Global rank of the city by cost of living (1 = highest cost) |
    18	| city | String | Name of the city |
    19	| country | String | Country where the city is located |
    20	| region | String | Geographic/economic region (e.g., Western Europe, Asia, Americas) |
    21	| cost_of_living_index | Float | Overall cost of living index relative to New York (100) |
    22	| rent_index | Float | Rent price index relative to New York (100) |
    23	| cost_of_living_plus_rent_index | Float | Combined cost of living and rent index relative to New York (100) |
    24	| groceries_index | Float | Grocery prices index relative to New York (100) |
    25	| restaurant_price_index | Float | Restaurant prices index relative to New York (100) |
    26	| local_purchasing_power_index | Float | Local purchasing power index relative to New York (100); higher values indicate greater purchasing power |
    27	| avg_monthly_net_salary_usd | Integer | Average monthly net salary in USD |
    28	| monthly_rent_1br_city_center_usd | Integer | Monthly rent for a 1-bedroom apartment in the city center, in USD |
    29	| monthly_rent_1br_outside_center_usd | Integer | Monthly rent for a 1-bedroom apartment outside the city center, in USD |
    30	| petrol_price_usd_per_liter | Float | Petrol (gasoline) price in USD per liter |
    31	| annual_inflation_rate_2025_pct | Float | Annual inflation rate as of 2025 (percentage) |
    32	| population_city_millions | Float | City population in millions |
    33	| cost_crisis_tier | Integer | Numeric tier classifying the severity of the cost-of-living crisis (lower values may indicate affluent/high-cost cities; higher values indicate more severe crisis conditions) |
    34	| crisis_label | String | Descriptive label for the crisis tier (e.g., "Affluent – High Cost", and other categories indicating varying levels of economic stress) |
    35	| oil_shock_exposure | String | Categorical assessment of the city's vulnerability to oil price shocks (e.g., "Low", "Medium", "High") |
    36	| rent_to_salary_ratio_pct | Float | Percentage of average monthly salary consumed by city-center 1BR rent; higher values indicate greater rent burden |
    37	| data_year | Integer | Year the data represents (all values are 2026) |
    38	| baseline_city | String | Reference city for all index calculations ("New York, USA (index=100)") |
    39	
    40	## Key Analytical Notes
    41	
    42	- **Index interpretation:** All index columns (cost_of_living_index, rent_index, groceries_index, restaurant_price_index, local_purchasing_power_index, and the combined index) are relative to New York City = 100. Values above 100 indicate higher costs (or greater purchasing power) than New York; values below 100 indicate lower.
    43	- **Crisis classification:** The `cost_crisis_tier` (integer) and `crisis_label` (string) columns together classify each city's economic stress level. Analysts should examine the distribution of these tiers to understand how many cities fall into each category.
    44	- **Rent burden:** The `rent_to_salary_ratio_pct` is a pre-calculated metric that directly measures housing affordability. Values above 50% are generally considered severe.
    45	- **Oil shock exposure:** This categorical variable (Low/Medium/High) can be cross-referenced with inflation and cost indices to assess vulnerability.
    46	- **Data quality:** The dataset is compiled for analytical and educational purposes and may include estimated or aggregated values. The `data_year` and `baseline_city` columns are constant across all rows (2026 and New York respectively). No missing values are indicated in the schema, but analysts should verify completeness during processing.
    47	- **Scope:** With 80 cities across multiple regions, the dataset enables both city-level deep dives and region-level aggregations.

import pandas as pd
import json

df = pd.read_csv('benchmark/data.csv')

# ===== KPIs =====
median_coli = df['cost_of_living_index'].median()
avg_rent_ratio = df['rent_to_salary_ratio_pct'].mean()
pp_gap = df['local_purchasing_power_index'].max() - df['local_purchasing_power_index'].min()
high_crisis_count = int((df['cost_crisis_tier'] == df['cost_crisis_tier'].max()).sum())
avg_inflation = df['annual_inflation_rate_2025_pct'].mean()

print("=== KPIs ===")
print(f"Median Cost of Living Index: {median_coli:.1f}")
print(f"Average Rent-to-Salary Ratio: {avg_rent_ratio:.1f}%")
print(f"Purchasing Power Gap: {pp_gap:.1f}")
print(f"High-Crisis City Count: {high_crisis_count}")
print(f"Average Annual Inflation Rate: {avg_inflation:.1f}%")

regional = df.groupby('region').agg(
    cities=('city','count'),
    median_coli=('cost_of_living_index','median'),
    mean_coli=('cost_of_living_index','mean'),
    median_rent_index=('rent_index','median'),
    mean_rent_index=('rent_index','mean'),
    median_purchasing_power=('local_purchasing_power_index','median'),
    mean_purchasing_power=('local_purchasing_power_index','mean'),
    median_rent_ratio=('rent_to_salary_ratio_pct','median'),
    mean_rent_ratio=('rent_to_salary_ratio_pct','mean'),
    mean_inflation=('annual_inflation_rate_2025_pct','mean'),
    median_inflation=('annual_inflation_rate_2025_pct','median'),
).round(2).sort_values('mean_coli', ascending=False)

print("\n=== Highest Inflation ===")

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import base64
from io import BytesIO
import json

df = pd.read_csv('benchmark/data.csv')

# Ensure output dir exists
import os
os.makedirs('/app/output', exist_ok=True)

charts = {}

# Helper to save chart as base64
def to_base64(fig):
    buf = BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buf, format='png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.close(fig)
    buf.seek(0)
    return base64.b64encode(buf.read()).decode('utf-8')

# 1. KPI summary horizontal bar (tier distribution)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4))
tier_counts = df['cost_crisis_tier'].value_counts().sort_index()
tier_labels = ['Tier 1\n(Affluent)', 'Tier 2\n(High Cost)', 'Tier 3\n(Moderate)', 'Tier 4\n(Low Income)', 'Tier 5\n(Severe Crisis)']
colors_tiers = ['#1e3a5f','#2e5984','#c9a227','#c45c26','#8b1e1e']
ax.barh(tier_labels, tier_counts.values, color=colors_tiers)
ax.set_xlabel('Number of Cities')
ax.set_title('City Distribution by Crisis Tier', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
for i,v in enumerate(tier_counts.values):
    ax.text(v+0.3, i, str(v), va='center', fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xlim(0, max(tier_counts.values)+5)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
charts['tier_distribution'] = to_base64(fig)

# 2. Regional comparison grouped bar (COLI, Rent Index, Purchasing Power)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10,5))
regional = df.groupby('region').agg(
    mean_coli=('cost_of_living_index','mean'),
    mean_rent=('rent_index','mean'),
    mean_pp=('local_purchasing_power_index','mean')
).sort_values('mean_coli', ascending=True)
regions = regional.index.tolist()
x = range(len(regions))
width = 0.25
ax.barh([i-width for i in x], regional['mean_coli'], width, label='Cost of Living Index', color='#1e3a5f')
ax.barh([i for i in x], regional['mean_rent'], width, label='Rent Index', color='#2e5984')
ax.barh([i+width for i in x], regional['mean_pp'], width, label='Purchasing Power Index', color='#4a8c6f')
ax.set_yticks(x)
ax.set_yticklabels(regions, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel('Index (NY = 100)')
ax.set_title('Regional Comparison: Cost of Living, Rent, and Purchasing Power', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax.legend(loc='lower right')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
charts['regional_comparison'] = to_base64(fig)

# 3. Rent Burden scatter (salary vs rent ratio, colored by tier)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10,6))
tier_color_map = {1:'#1e3a5f', 2:'#2e5984', 3:'#c9a227', 4:'#c45c26', 5:'#8b1e1e'}
for tier in sorted(df['cost_crisis_tier'].unique()):
    sub = df[df['cost_crisis_tier']==tier]
    ax.scatter(sub['avg_monthly_net_salary_usd'], sub['rent_to_salary_ratio_pct'],
               c=tier_color_map[tier], label=f'Tier {tier}', s=80, alpha=0.85, edgecolors='white', linewidth=0.5)
# Annotate extremes
for _, row in df.nlargest(5, 'rent_to_salary_ratio_pct').iterrows():
    ax.annotate(row['city'], (row['avg_monthly_net_salary_usd'], row['rent_to_salary_ratio_pct']),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(5,-8), fontsize=8, color='#333')
for _, row in df.nsmallest(5, 'rent_to_salary_ratio_pct').iterrows():
    ax.annotate(row['city'], (row['avg_monthly_net_salary_usd'], row['rent_to_salary_ratio_pct']),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(5,5), fontsize=8, color='#333')
ax.axhline(y=50, color='#8b1e1e', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, alpha=0.7, label='50% threshold')
ax.set_xlabel('Average Monthly Net Salary (USD)')
ax.set_ylabel('Rent-to-Salary Ratio (%)')
ax.set_title('Rent Burden vs. Income Level by Crisis Tier', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax.legend(title='Crisis Tier', loc='upper right', fontsize=8)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
charts['rent_burden_scatter'] = to_base64(fig)

# 4. Top 15 rent burden cities horizontal bar
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8,7))
top_rent = df.nlargest(15, 'rent_to_salary_ratio_pct')[['city','rent_to_salary_ratio_pct','cost_crisis_tier']].sort_values('rent_to_salary_ratio_pct')
bar_colors = [tier_color_map[t] for t in top_rent['cost_crisis_tier']]
ax.barh(top_rent['city'], top_rent['rent_to_salary_ratio_pct'], color=bar_colors)
ax.set_xlabel('Rent-to-Salary Ratio (%)')
ax.set_title('Top 15 Cities by Rent Burden', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
for i,v in enumerate(top_rent['rent_to_salary_ratio_pct']):
    ax.text(v+0.3, i, f"{v:.1f}%", va='center', fontsize=9)

ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
charts['top_rent_burden'] = to_base64(fig)

    mean_coli=('cost_of_living_index','mean'),
    mean_rent=('rent_index','mean'),
    mean_rent_ratio=('rent_to_salary_ratio_pct','mean'),
    mean_pp=('local_purchasing_power_index','mean'),
    mean_inflation=('annual_inflation_rate_2025_pct','mean'),
    mean_groceries=('groceries_index','mean')

# Normalize for radar-like comparison (scale 0-100 roughly)
metrics = ['mean_coli','mean_rent','mean_rent_ratio','mean_pp','mean_inflation','mean_groceries']
metric_labels = ['Cost of Living','Rent Index','Rent Ratio (%)','Purchasing Power','Inflation (%)','Groceries']
# Use grouped bar instead of radar for clarity
x = range(len(metric_labels))
width = 0.15
colors_tiers = ['#1e3a5f','#2e5984','#c9a227','#c45c26','#8b1e1e']
for idx, row in tier_profile.iterrows():
    vals = [row[m] for m in metrics]
    ax.bar([i + idx*width for i in x], vals, width, label=f"Tier {int(row['cost_crisis_tier'])}", color=colors_tiers[idx])
ax.set_xticks([i + 2*width for i in x])
ax.set_xticklabels(metric_labels, rotation=15, ha='right')
ax.set_ylabel('Index / Percentage Value')
ax.set_title('Average Indicators by Crisis Tier', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax.legend(title='Crisis Tier')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
charts['tier_profile'] = to_base64(fig)

# 6. Inflation vs Oil Shock Exposure grouped bar
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8,5))
oil_inf = df.groupby('oil_shock_exposure')['annual_inflation_rate_2025_pct'].mean().reindex(['Low','Medium','High'])
ax.bar(oil_inf.index, oil_inf.values, color=['#4a8c6f','#c9a227','#8b1e1e'])
ax.set_ylabel('Average Annual Inflation Rate (%)')
ax.set_title('Average Inflation Rate by Oil Shock Exposure', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
for i,v in enumerate(oil_inf.values):
    ax.text(i, v+0.5, f"{v:.1f}%", ha='center', fontweight='bold')
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False)
ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
charts['oil_inflation'] = to_base64(fig)

# 7. Oil shock vs purchasing power scatter
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8,5))
for exposure, color in zip(['Low','Medium','High'], ['#4a8c6f','#c9a227','#8b1e1e']):
    sub = df[df['oil_shock_exposure']==exposure]
    ax.scatter(sub['annual_inflation_rate_2025_pct'], sub['local_purchasing_power_index'],

# annotate extreme inflation cities
for _, row in df.nlargest(5, 'annual_inflation_rate_2025_pct').iterrows():

ax.legend(title='Oil Shock Exposure')

Key Findings

  1. The crisis is not evenly distributed. Fourteen cities (Tier 5) face severe affordability crises, but they are concentrated in South Asia, Africa, and conflict zones. Another 12 cities (Tier 4) are structurally vulnerable.

  3. Purchasing power is the great divider. The gap between the highest (Basel, 183.7) and lowest (Beirut, 35.0) purchasing power indices is {pp_gap:.1f} points—nearly a 5:1 ratio. Cost of living alone is a poor proxy for economic stress.
  4. Oil shock exposure amplifies inflation risk. High-exposure cities average 20.4% inflation. For import-dependent economies, energy transition and strategic reserves are cost-of-living policies.
  5. Regional outliers need tailored responses. Singapore, Tel Aviv, and Hong Kong face unique cost pressures that regional averages obscure. One-size-fits-all regional policy will fail these cities.

Cities and Regions Requiring Urgent Attention

Tier 5 – Immediate Intervention: Buenos Aires, Beirut, Karachi, Lahore, Cairo, Lagos, Dhaka, Kathmandu, Colombo, Accra, Kyiv, and others. These cities require coordinated support spanning macroeconomic stabilization, social protection, and humanitarian assistance.
Tier 4 – Structural Support: Nairobi, St Petersburg, Hanoi, Jakarta, and similar cities need investment in wage growth, currency stability, and affordable housing finance.

  • Housing policy must be income-sensitive. Rent control and social housing are critical in low-income, high-density cities. In high-wage cities, zoning reform and supply expansion are more effective.
  • Inflation targeting is a cost-of-living policy. Central banks in high-crisis cities should prioritize currency stability and food-price monitoring.
  • Energy security reduces living-cost volatility. Diversifying energy sources and building strategic reserves can buffer oil-shock exposure.
  • Purchasing power data should complement cost indices. Policymakers should report affordability as a ratio of cost to income, not cost alone.
  • Cross-border coordination is essential for outliers. Cities like Singapore and Hong Kong, which are global financial hubs with local housing shortages, need supra-national policy frameworks for capital flows and land use.

  • Longitudinal tracking of rent-to-salary ratios to identify tipping points into crisis tiers.
  • Disaggregated data by income decile within cities—averages mask extreme inequality.
  • Impact of remittance flows on purchasing power in South Asian and African cities.
  • Effectiveness of rent-control policies across different crisis tiers.

  • Hong Kong (East Asia, COLI 75.2) is the region’s most expensive city, 15.2 points above the regional median, driven by extreme land scarcity and rent pressure.
Figure 3. Cities with the largest positive or negative deviation from their regional median cost of living. Positive values (red) indicate cities far more expensive than their region; negative values (blue) indicate cities cheaper than regional norms.

Latin America deserves special mention: its mean inflation rate is 34.2%, driven almost entirely by Buenos Aires (150.0%), which single-handedly distorts the regional average. Excluding Buenos Aires, Latin America’s mean inflation drops to approximately 5.5%.

Affordability and Rent Burden Analysis

Housing affordability—measured by the rent-to-salary ratio—is the single most actionable metric for policymakers. Globally, the average city-center 1-bedroom rent consumes {avg_rent_ratio:.1f}% of the average monthly net salary. No city in the dataset falls below 50%, confirming that rent burden is a universal feature of urban life in 2026.

Critical threshold: Ratios above 65% are common in high-cost cities (Zurich 70.8%, Geneva 70.2%, Seattle 71.2%). Ratios above 68% appear in 9 cities, all in Tier 1 or Tier 2. In low-income cities, ratios cluster between 51% and 58%—lower in percentage terms, but far more damaging in real terms because absolute residual income is tiny.
Figure 4. Rent-to-salary ratio versus average monthly net salary, colored by crisis tier. The dashed line marks the 50% threshold. High-income cities (right) often have ratios above 68%; low-income cities (left) cluster near 52–58% but leave almost no disposable income.

Cities with the Highest Rent Burden

The top 10 most rent-burdened cities are dominated by Switzerland and the United States:

{df_to_html(highest_rent_burden)}
Figure 5. Top 15 cities by rent-to-salary ratio. Swiss and US cities dominate, with ratios consistently above 67%.

Cities with the Lowest Rent Burden

At the other extreme, South Asian and African cities show the lowest ratios—but this is deceptive:

{df_to_html(lowest_rent_burden)}

While Lahore’s ratio is only 51.0%, its average net salary is $320/month and city-center rent is $245/month—leaving just $75 for all other expenses. By contrast, Seattle’s 71.2% ratio on a $6,200 salary leaves $1,783—more than five times Lahore’s total income. Policy interventions must therefore distinguish between percentage burden and absolute residual poverty.

Structural Drivers of Rent Burden

Two structural patterns emerge:

  • High-cost, high-wage cities (e.g., Zurich, San Francisco, Seattle): Rent is high in absolute terms, but salaries are high enough that residual income remains substantial. The policy challenge here is middle-class affordability and talent retention.
  • Low-cost, low-wage cities (e.g., Lahore, Dhaka, Cairo): Nominal rents are low, but wages are lower still. The policy challenge is absolute poverty, informal housing, and lack of social safety nets.

Crisis Tier Profiling

The five crisis tiers reveal distinct economic archetypes. Understanding what separates Tier 1 from Tier 5 is essential for targeting interventions.

Figure 6. Average indicators by crisis tier. Tier 1 shows high costs but very high purchasing power and low inflation. Tier 5 shows low nominal costs but collapsing purchasing power and extreme inflation.

Tier 1: Affluent – High Cost ({tier_counts[1]} cities)

All five Swiss cities (Zurich, Geneva, Basel, Lausanne, Bern) plus Dubai and Taipei fall here. Mean COLI is 113.8, but mean purchasing power is 168.9 and mean inflation is only 1.2%. These cities are expensive but prosperous. Rent burden is high (69.5% average) yet manageable due to salaries averaging $7,017.

Tier 2: High Cost – Mixed Compensation ({tier_counts[2]} cities)

This is the largest and most diverse tier. It includes global benchmarks (New York), high-wage tech hubs (San Francisco, Seattle), high-cost European capitals (London, Amsterdam), and cities with manageable costs but strong PPP (Copenhagen, Oslo). Mean COLI is 80.5, mean purchasing power 126.9, and rent burden averages 67.0%. The heterogeneity means policy prescriptions must be city-specific.

Tier 3: Moderate Cost – Transition Stress ({tier_counts[3]} cities)

Tier 3 cities span emerging markets and slowing economies. Mean COLI drops to 58.0, but purchasing power falls to 95.0 and inflation averages 2.8%. Notable cities include Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok, Mexico City, and Johannesburg. These cities are at an inflection point: costs are rising faster than wages, and housing stress is intensifying.

Tier 4: Low Income – Structural Vulnerability ({tier_counts[4]} cities)

Mean COLI is 45.0, but purchasing power is only 68.5 and salaries average $1,000/month. Cities like Nairobi, Accra, and St Petersburg face currency weakness, sanctions exposure, or commodity dependence. Inflation is moderate on average (9.5%) but highly variable.

Tier 5: Severe Crisis ({tier_counts[5]} cities)

The acute cohort. Mean COLI is just 32.0, but purchasing power collapses to 54.8 and inflation averages 5.9%—a figure masked by extreme outliers (Buenos Aires 150%, Beirut 50%). Salaries average only $537/month. These are the cities requiring urgent, multi-lateral policy attention:

{df_to_html(high_crisis_cities)}
Urgent attention required: Buenos Aires (150% inflation), Beirut (50% inflation, 35.0 PPP), and Karachi/Lahore/Cairo (hyperinflation + severe affordability crisis) represent the most acute cases. In these cities, cost-of-living policy is inseparable from macroeconomic stabilization and humanitarian support.

Inflation and Oil Shock Exposure

External economic shocks—particularly oil price volatility—interact with domestic inflation to create compounding stress. The dataset classifies cities into Low, Medium, and High oil shock exposure.

Oil Shock Exposure Profile

{df_to_html(oil_summary)}
Figure 7. Average inflation by oil shock exposure. High-exposure cities face inflation nearly 6× that of low-exposure cities.

Cities with High oil shock exposure (23 cities) have dramatically worse macroeconomic conditions: average inflation is 20.4% versus 3.4% for Low-exposure cities. Their mean purchasing power is only 67.8, compared to 128.6 for Low-exposure cities. This is not merely correlation—many high-exposure cities are import-dependent emerging markets where oil price spikes transmit directly into transport, food, and electricity costs.

Figure 8. Purchasing power versus inflation, colored by oil shock exposure. High-exposure cities (red) cluster in the lower-right quadrant—low purchasing power, high inflation.

Highest Inflation Cities

{df_to_html(highest_inflation)}

The inflation leaderboard is dominated by three distinct shock types:

  • Currency collapse / hyperinflation: Buenos Aires (150.0%), Istanbul (47.0%), Lagos (34.0%), Cairo (28.0%).
  • Conflict and sanctions: Beirut (50.0%), Kyiv (14.5%), Karachi/Lahore (28.5%).
  • Post-crisis adjustment: Colombo (14.0%), Accra (18.0%).

Notably, oil shock exposure is not the sole driver of inflation. Buenos Aires has Medium exposure but 150% inflation—driven by monetary policy and debt crisis. Conversely, Singapore has High exposure but only 2.3% inflation, thanks to strong fiscal buffers and currency management. Exposure is a risk factor, not a destiny.

Key Findings and Policy Implications

Key Findings

  1. The crisis is not evenly distributed. Fourteen cities (Tier 5) face severe affordability crises, but they are concentrated in South Asia, Africa, and conflict zones. Another 12 cities (Tier 4) are structurally vulnerable.
  2. Rent burden is universal but qualitatively different. Every city in the dataset exceeds the 50% threshold. In high-wage cities, the challenge is quality of life and savings; in low-wage cities, it is survival.
  3. Purchasing power is the great divider. The gap between the highest (Basel, 183.7) and lowest (Beirut, 35.0) purchasing power indices is {pp_gap:.1f} points—nearly a 5:1 ratio. Cost of living alone is a poor proxy for economic stress.
  4. Oil shock exposure amplifies inflation risk. High-exposure cities average 20.4% inflation. For import-dependent economies, energy transition and strategic reserves are cost-of-living policies.
  5. Regional outliers need tailored responses. Singapore, Tel Aviv, and Hong Kong face unique cost pressures that regional averages obscure. One-size-fits-all regional policy will fail these cities.

Cities and Regions Requiring Urgent Attention

Tier 5 – Immediate Intervention: Buenos Aires, Beirut, Karachi, Lahore, Cairo, Lagos, Dhaka, Kathmandu, Colombo, Accra, Kyiv, and others. These cities require coordinated support spanning macroeconomic stabilization, social protection, and humanitarian assistance.
Tier 4 – Structural Support: Nairobi, St Petersburg, Hanoi, Jakarta, and similar cities need investment in wage growth, currency stability, and affordable housing finance.

Policy Implications

  • Housing policy must be income-sensitive. Rent control and social housing are critical in low-income, high-density cities. In high-wage cities, zoning reform and supply expansion are more effective.
  • Inflation targeting is a cost-of-living policy. Central banks in high-crisis cities should prioritize currency stability and food-price monitoring.
  • Energy security reduces living-cost volatility. Diversifying energy sources and building strategic reserves can buffer oil-shock exposure.
  • Purchasing power data should complement cost indices. Policymakers should report affordability as a ratio of cost to income, not cost alone.
  • Cross-border coordination is essential for outliers. Cities like Singapore and Hong Kong, which are global financial hubs with local housing shortages, need supra-national policy frameworks for capital flows and land use.

Areas for Further Research

  • Longitudinal tracking of rent-to-salary ratios to identify tipping points into crisis tiers.
  • Disaggregated data by income decile within cities—averages mask extreme inequality.
  • Impact of remittance flows on purchasing power in South Asian and African cities.
  • Effectiveness of rent-control policies across different crisis tiers.
